diagnostic_evidence.quote: Wahba's problem aims at finding a nonzero quaternion $\qq$ that minimizes the cost function

The presented results offer a complete theoretical characterisation of the Wahba problem in quaternions and lay a rigorous foundation for further generalisations in quaternion-based orientation estimation.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper defines Wahba's problem as minimization, but its results address only existence and parameterization of zero-cost solutions. They supply no minimizer when the two pairs are not jointly similar. For example, observations (i,j) and (2i,j) have minimum cost 1, attained at q=1, and are outside the zero-cost results. The unqualified two-observation solution and complete-characterization claims therefore exceed the established scope.

failure_location.quote: In this paper, we solve the Wahba's problem for the special and practically important case $\ell = 2$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the solution and characterization claims throughout to the zero-cost, pairwise-similar two-observation subclass. Retaining the broader claim requires an additional method and proof for positive-cost minimizers.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised optimization guarantee is unsupported for positive-minimum instances, including inconsistent observations.
issues.title: Zero-cost feasibility is advertised as solving the general two-observation minimization problem
issues.why_classification: The source-supported restriction abandons the advertised minimization guarantee for an entire regime, changing the guarantee from general optimization to zero-cost feasibility.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Nonreal quaternions $\qa,\qb$ are similar if and only if
Then, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:SIMILAR_QUATERNIONS_CHARACTERIZATION} and the property in~\eqref{eq:NORM_OF_QUAT_SUM} we obtain

issues.failure_explanation: Nonreal summands can have real sums. For example, a1=i, a2=−i, b1=j, b2=−j satisfy the hypotheses and are jointly conjugate, but both sums are zero. The displayed similarity assertion is then outside the stated definition, and the subsequent nonreal-quaternion characterization is invoked outside its hypotheses. The converse repeats the same domain problem.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Obtain the forward norm equality directly from multiplicativity. Handle real sums separately in the converse: equal real parts and equal norms imply that both sums are the same real scalar, which any nonzero quaternion conjugates to itself.
issues.overall_effect: The proof does not validly cover permitted inputs whose imaginary components cancel in the sums.
issues.title: Similarity is applied to sums that need not be nonreal
issues.why_classification: A short real-sum case distinction and direct norm calculation preserve the statement and its full scope without a new nontrivial argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Set $\qq = \qq[1]\qq[2]$, where $\qq[2]$ is a nonzero quaternion such that $\qb[1]\qq[2] = \qq[2]\qb[1]$.

issues.failure_explanation: A conjugator of the sums is first obtained, but q is subsequently reset to q1q2 with q2 merely commuting with b1. This ensures the first alignment, not the earlier sum alignment. For a1=b1=i, a2=j, b2=k, the choice q1=q2=1 satisfies the stated construction conditions but does not align the sums. Existence of a commuting q2 that also preserves the sum equation is the missing substantive step.

failure_location.quote: Substituting \eqref{eq:PAIRWISE_SIMILARITY_PROOF_PART_1} into \eqref{eq:SUM_SIMILARITY} yields $\qq[][-1]\qa[2]\qq[] = \qb[2]$, which completes the proof.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a centralizer-alignment argument: after q1 aligns the first imaginary components, show that the second components have equal projections on Im b1 and equal perpendicular lengths, then construct a quaternion commuting with b1 that aligns those perpendicular components, including zero and opposite cases.
issues.overall_effect: The sufficiency direction of the advertised scalar characterization of pairwise similarity is unproved.
issues.title: The pairwise-similarity converse never establishes a common conjugator
issues.why_classification: The repair requires a contained nontrivial existence construction, but preserves the criterion without changing the paper's overall proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: A quaternion $\qa$ is called unit if $\Abs{\qa} = 1$ and it is called pure if $\rea = 0$.

issues.failure_explanation: Zero is pure under the stated definition. Thus, for example, a=−1 and the permitted parameter p=0 make the asserted formula contain 0/0. The negative-real branch is not defined on its declared auxiliary parameter domain.

failure_location.quote:
where $\qp$ is either an arbitrary pure quaternion if $\qa$ is a negative real

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require p to be a nonzero pure quaternion in the negative-real case.
issues.overall_effect: The square-root formula admits an undefined parameter choice, although every actual square root remains obtainable using nonzero pure parameters.
issues.title: The square-root parameterization allows division by zero
issues.why_classification: The local domain restriction excludes no actual solution and changes neither the construction nor its substantive coverage.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses allow collinear imaginary observations, so the auxiliary a3 and b3 can both be zero, outside the nonreal Sylvester framework. Taking a1=b1=i and a2=b2=2i gives zero cost at q=1, but both cross products vanish. The proposed q2 is therefore λ2√0=0, making q=q1q2=0 and its inverse undefined. Thus the formula produces no valid solution for this allowed case.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a zero-cross-product branch: set q2=1 and use the established single-observation parameterization q=q1. Pairwise similarity makes the second alignment redundant in this case. Apply the two-stage square-root formula only when the cross products are nonzero.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed general solution omits all solutions for compatible collinear observation pairs.
issues.title: Collinear observations make the proposed quaternion identically zero
issues.why_classification: A routine degenerate-case branch using an already established result restores every claimed solution without narrowing scope or changing the closed-form method.

issues.failure_explanation: The square-root contribution cannot be discarded from the commutation constraint for all advertised root choices. When a3=−b3≠0, the radicand is negative real, and its pure square roots need not commute with b1. For a1=b1=i, a2=j, b2=−j, the pairs are jointly conjugate via i. Nevertheless, q1=1, λ2=1, q2=j satisfy the displayed square-root formula and k·j=0 side condition. Their product q=j sends i to −i and has cost 8, not zero.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: For nonzero C=q1^{-1}(Im a1×Im a2)q1 and D=Im b1×Im b2, handle C=−D by taking q2 to be a nonzero real multiple of Im b1. Retain the existing root formula otherwise. Use this normalized antiparallel test, or test for a negative-real radicand, so rescaling q1 cannot suppress the branch.
issues.overall_effect: The parameterization includes non-solutions even for noncollinear, exactly compatible observations.
issues.title: Antiparallel residuals admit square roots that destroy the first alignment
issues.why_classification: The missing branch follows by routine algebra from the commutation and anticommutation relations already established in the proof. It preserves the full solution set, scope, and closed-form guarantee.
